data.summary: Connective tissue diseases · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Striae distensae** (Connective tissue diseases)_

**Q1. What are striae distensae?**
- Linear dermal scars with epidermal atrophy due to stretching and changes in dermal connective tissue (stretch marks)
- Early: striae rubrae (red/purple, raised, inflamed); late: striae albae (white, atrophic, wrinkled, depressed)

**Q2. Causes.**
- Physiological: puberty (adolescent growth spurt — thighs, buttocks, breasts, lower back), pregnancy (striae gravidarum — up to 90%, abdomen, breasts, thighs; PYQ in physiological changes of pregnancy), weight gain/obesity, body-building
- Pathological: Cushing's syndrome (wide >1 cm, purple, also on unusual sites), prolonged topical or systemic corticosteroids (especially potent steroids under occlusion in flexures — groin, axilla, inner thighs), Marfan syndrome, Ehlers–Danlos, anorexia nervosa recovery, chronic liver disease, HIV (protease inhibitors), diabetes

**Q3. Pathogenesis.**
- Mechanical stretch + hormonal influence (glucocorticoids, oestrogen, relaxin) → fibroblast dysfunction, fragmentation and loss of elastic fibres and fibrillin, reduced collagen synthesis → rupture of dermal connective tissue
- Genetic predisposition (family history, fibrillin/elastin/collagen gene variants)

**Q4. Histopathology.**
- Early: dermal oedema, perivascular lymphocytes, elastolysis
- Late: thinned epidermis with flattened rete ridges, thin straight collagen bundles parallel to skin surface (like a scar), reduced and curled elastic fibres, loss of adnexa

**Q5. Differential diagnosis.**
- Linear focal elastosis (yellow palpable striae on lower back of elderly men), anetoderma, atrophic scars, linear atrophoderma of Moulin, linear morphoea
- Cushing's striae vs physiological: wide, deep purple, beyond usual sites (shoulders, axillae), with other Cushingoid features — screen with cortisol tests

**Q6. Treatment.**
- Prevention: no strong evidence; massage with emollients (centella asiatica, hyaluronic acid) may help in pregnancy
- Striae rubrae respond better: topical tretinoin 0.05–0.1% (not in pregnancy/lactation), hyaluronic acid, pulsed-dye laser 585/595 nm, IPL
- Striae albae: microneedling (± PRP), fractional non-ablative (1550 nm) or ablative (CO2, Er:YAG) lasers, radiofrequency, microdermabrasion, excimer laser (repigmentation), chemical peels (glycolic/TCA)
- Counsel: improvement (not complete removal) is the realistic goal; treat cause (stop steroids, Cushing's)

**Q7. How do striae of Cushing's syndrome differ?**
- Wide (>1 cm), deep purple-red, depressed, on abdomen, flanks, thighs, axillae, breasts; associated central obesity, moon face, buffalo hump, thin skin, bruising, proximal myopathy, hypertension, hyperglycaemia — confirm with overnight dexamethasone suppression test, 24-h urinary cortisol, late-night salivary cortisol

**Q8. What does dermoscopy show?**
- Rubrae: pink-red streaks with linear/dotted vessels; Albae: white, atrophic linear bands with absent pigment network and skin markings parallel to the long axis

**Q9. Topical steroid-induced striae — prevention.**
- Avoid potent steroids on flexures, face, groin, and under occlusion; limit duration; use fingertip units; prefer calcineurin inhibitors on thin skin; striae once formed are permanent

**Q10. What are the risk factors for striae gravidarum?**
- Young maternal age, family history, high pre-pregnancy BMI and weight gain, large baby/ macrosomia, polyhydramnios, multiple pregnancy, lighter skin type; appear in second half of pregnancy on abdomen, breasts, hips, thighs

**Q11. What is the role of topical tretinoin and its limitations?**
- Tretinoin 0.05–0.1% nightly improves early striae rubrae (stimulates collagen synthesis, fibroblast activity); contraindicated in pregnancy and avoided during breastfeeding; little effect on mature striae albae

**Q12. Explain fractional lasers in striae.**
- Fractional photothermolysis creates microscopic thermal zones → neocollagenesis and remodelling; non-ablative 1550 nm (fewer side effects) and ablative CO2/Er:YAG (better efficacy, more PIH in dark skin); 3–6 sessions; combine with PRP/ radiofrequency

**Q13. Striae in adolescents — counselling.**
- Very common during growth spurts (boys — lumbosacral, thighs; girls — breasts, thighs, buttocks); harmless, fade to white with time; rule out steroid misuse (gym supplements, topical creams) and Cushing's if severe/ atypical

**Q14. Linear focal elastosis — what is it?**
- Elastotic striae: palpable yellow linear bands on lower back of elderly men — increased, fragmented elastic fibres in dermis (differs from striae with reduced elastin); considered a keloidal repair of striae

**Q15. Striae in Marfan syndrome — significance.**
- Striae in unusual sites (shoulders, lower back) without weight change is a minor criterion in Marfan syndrome (FBN1); look for tall stature, arachnodactyly, lens dislocation, aortic root dilatation

## Quick spotter facts
- Wide purple striae on unusual sites — think Cushing's/steroids
- Striae rubrae respond better than striae albae

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Dermal disorders; physiological skin changes in pregnancy). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
